intro: This guide takes your group through The Pilgrim’s Progress (For Children) in twelve weeks, one short chapter each week. It’s written for children aged about 6 to 12 and works just as well for a Sunday school class, a homeschool co-op or a family around the kitchen table. Christian’s journey from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City is an adventure story, and every scene pictures something true about following God.

Each session takes about 30 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter aloud (5–7 minutes). Talk together using the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (5–10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close by praying the chapter’s short prayer, or one of your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand so you can read it with expression, and glance at the activity so you know what you’ll need. Most weeks need nothing more than paper and crayons or pencils, and some need nothing at all. Keep it warm and unhurried: if the children are enjoying the talk, it’s fine to shorten the activity.

weeks.summary: Christian lives in the City of Destruction and is crushed by a heavy burden on his back that he cannot get off. Evangelist points him toward a little gate and a shining light, and Christian runs for it with his fingers in his ears, crying, “Life! Life! Eternal life!” The big idea: when we see that something is wrong inside us, we don’t have to carry it alone — we can run to Jesus, the true Light.

memory_verse.text: Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your house.

activity.title: Run to the Light
activity.materials: One sheet of paper with a big yellow sun or light drawn on it
steps: Prop up or hold up the “light” picture at one end of the room and gather the children at the other end.
Explain that they are Christian, running to the light, and that nothing must turn them aside.
Have everyone put their fingers in their ears and walk slowly toward the light while you call out silly distractions like “Come back and play!”
When they reach the light, let everyone shout together, “Life! Life! Eternal life!”
Sit down and ask: who is the true Light the story says we can run to?

weeks.summary: Hurrying toward the light, Christian falls into the Slough of Despond, the Swamp of Feeling Hopeless, and his burden drags him deeper. His neighbour Pliable climbs out and goes home, leaving him alone, until a man called Help reaches down, says, “Give me your hand,” and pulls him onto solid ground. The big idea: everyone feels stuck and hopeless sometimes, but we aren’t meant to climb out alone — God reaches out to help us.

memory_verse.text: He brought me up also out of a horrible pit, out of the miry clay. He set my feet on a rock, and gave me a firm place to stand.

activity.title: Give Me Your Hand
steps: Put the children in pairs or threes, all at the same time, so no one is on show.
One child in each group crouches low and pretends to sink slowly into sticky mud, pulling heavy feet up and down.
The other says, “Give me your hand,” and gently helps them stand up on “solid ground.”
Swap roles so everyone gets to be both Christian and Help.
Ask: who does God send to help us when we feel stuck?

weeks.summary: Christian reaches the little gate with the words “Knock, and it shall be opened to you” above it. He knocks, worried he might not be let in, but Goodwill opens the gate wide, welcomes him with all his heart and sets him on the narrow path, telling him his burden will fall off at the right place. The big idea: God never turns away anyone who comes to him — we don’t have to be good enough first, we just have to knock.

memory_verse.text: Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened to you.

activity.title: A Door That Opens
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half like a card, so the front flap opens like a door.
On the front, draw a little gate or door with a door knocker.
Inside, draw a welcoming face and write “Come in!” or “Welcome!”
Practise knocking on the front of the card, then open it, saying the memory verse together.

weeks.summary: At the Interpreter’s house, Christian is shown rooms full of wonders. A dusty room only gets dustier when swept until water is sprinkled on it, and a fire keeps burning even when water is thrown on it, because a hidden man pours oil on it. The Interpreter explains that rules alone stir up sin but the good news of Jesus makes hearts clean, and that Jesus secretly keeps faith burning in us. The big idea: God loves to open our eyes so we understand how things really work on the inside.

memory_verse.text: Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.

activity.title: Two Wonderful Rooms
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half to make two “rooms.”
In the first room, draw the dusty parlour: the dust flying up when it is swept, then the girl sprinkling water.
In the second room, draw the fire with water thrown on one side and the hidden man pouring oil on the other.
Show your pictures to a neighbour and tell each other what the Interpreter said each room means.

weeks.summary: Christian comes to the Cross, and the moment he reaches it, his burden comes loose, rolls down the hill into an open tomb and is gone for good. He weeps for joy and leaps three times, and three Shining Ones tell him his sins are forgiven, give him new clothes, and give him a mark and a letter for the gate of the City. The big idea: we can’t lift our own load of wrongdoing, but Jesus takes it away at the Cross — the best news there is.

memory_verse.text: Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.

activity.title: The Burden Rolls Away
activity.materials: One sheet of scrap paper per child
steps: Give each child a blank sheet of paper to scrunch into a ball — this is Christian’s burden. Nobody writes anything on it.
Have everyone walk around the room bent over, as if the burden is very heavy on their backs.
Point to one spot in the room as the Cross and another corner as the open tomb.
When each child reaches the Cross, they roll their burden into the tomb corner and give three big leaps for joy.
Gather the paper balls for recycling and ask: who is the only one who can take our burden away?

weeks.summary: Christian climbs the steep Hill Difficulty on hands and knees, falls asleep in the shelter and loses his precious letter, and has to go back down to find it. Near the top two lions roar, but a watchman tells him they are chained, so he walks safely down the middle of the path to the Palace Beautiful, where he is fed, rested and dressed in shining armour. The big idea: following God can be hard work, and some scary things are chained, but God gives us rest, friends and armour for the road.

memory_verse.text: Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.

activity.title: Between the Chained Lions
steps: Choose two or three volunteers at a time to be the chained lions, standing on either side of a “path” across the room.
The lions may roar and paw the air, but must keep their feet still because they are chained.
Everyone else walks one by one down the middle of the path, while you call out like the watchman, “Don’t be afraid — keep to the middle!”
Swap the lions often so everyone who wants a turn gets one.
Ask: what did the women at the Palace Beautiful give Christian for the road ahead?

weeks.summary: In a low valley the dragon-like monster Apollyon claims Christian belongs to him and attacks with flaming darts. They fight for half a day, Christian is wounded and loses his sword, but he grabs it again, cries, “When I fall, I will get up again!” and declares that we are more than conquerors through Jesus, and Apollyon flies away. The big idea: we don’t beat the enemy in our own strength — when we say no to what’s wrong and hold on to God’s Word and Jesus, the enemy runs.

memory_verse.text: Be subject therefore to God. But resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

activity.title: Say Yes or Say No
steps: Name one side of the room “Yes, do it!” and the other side “Say no!”
Read out simple everyday choices, such as “A friend says, let’s take a sweet without asking,” or “Your sister needs help tidying up.”
After each one, everyone walks to the side they think is right.
For each “Say no!” choice, shout together, “Resist the devil, and he will flee!”
Ask: what did Christian use to win, and what can help us say no?

weeks.summary: In the Valley of the Shadow of Death it is so dark Christian can hardly see where to step, and his sword is no use. He uses the best weapon of all, All-prayer, crying, “O Lord, save me!” Even when a creature whispers nasty thoughts in his ear, he hears another traveller ahead saying Psalm 23 and realises he isn’t alone, and morning comes. The big idea: when life feels dark and scary, the simplest and best thing to do is pray, because God is with us in the dark.

memory_verse.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.

activity.title: All-Prayer Lanterns
steps: Give each child paper and invite them to draw a lantern glowing in a dark valley, colouring the dark all around it.
Inside the lantern’s light, they can write or draw one thing they’d like to talk to God about. This stays private — no one has to show it.
Gather quietly and, if you can, dim the lights a little.
Invite everyone to hold their lantern and pray silently for a minute, then close by saying the memory verse together softly.

weeks.summary: Christian and his brave friend Faithful pass through Vanity Fair, a town that cares only for shiny things, and answer the sellers, “We buy the truth.” The angry crowd mocks them and locks them up, and Faithful is put on an unfair trial, but he keeps trusting God and is carried straight up to the gates of the City. Christian escapes and Hopeful joins him, because he saw how bravely they loved God. The big idea: staying faithful to God can cost something, but God sees, remembers and rewards it.

memory_verse.text: Let us not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.

activity.title: What Will You Buy?
activity.materials: One large sheet of paper and crayons or a pencil
steps: Draw a line down the middle of a large sheet of paper.
Label one side “Shiny things at the fair” and the other “Things that really last.”
Let the children call out ideas for each side (toys, gadgets, being famous; truth, kindness, friendship, loving God) while you or an older child writes them down.
Read both lists aloud, then all shout Christian and Faithful’s answer together: “We buy the truth!”

weeks.summary: Christian and Hopeful leave the narrow path for an easier-looking meadow, get lost in a storm and are caught by Giant Despair, who throws them into the dungeon of Doubting Castle and tells them to give up hope. Hopeful keeps encouraging Christian, they pray, and Christian suddenly remembers he has had a key called Promise in his pocket all along, which opens every lock. The big idea: when we feel trapped and hopeless, God’s promises in the Bible are the key that sets us free.

memory_verse.text: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope unyieldingly. For he who promised is faithful.

activity.title: The Key Called Promise
steps: Draw a big, fancy key that fills most of a sheet of paper.
Write “Promise” on the handle of the key.
Along the long part of the key, copy one of God’s promises from this book, such as “I will give you rest” or “I am with you.”
Decorate the key, then take it home to keep somewhere you’ll see it when you feel sad.

weeks.summary: Christian and Hopeful rest on the Delectable Mountains, where four kind shepherds named Knowledge, Experience, Watchful and Sincere feed them and show them wonders and warnings about travellers who left the path. From a hill called Clear, through a special telescope, the pilgrims glimpse the gate of the Celestial City, and the shepherds warn them to keep watching. The big idea: God is our good Shepherd, who feeds us, warns us of danger and lets us catch sight of the home he is bringing us to.

memory_verse.text: The LORD is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.

activity.title: Glimpse the City
steps: Together, draw the Celestial City on one or two big sheets: shining walls, a golden gate, bright light.
Put the picture up on the far side of the room.
Each child rolls a sheet of paper into a tube to make a telescope.
Stand on the “hill called Clear” and take turns looking through your telescopes at the City.
Ask: what did the good shepherds do for the pilgrims, and how is God like them?

weeks.summary: At the very end, Christian and Hopeful must cross a deep river with no bridge to reach the shining City. Christian begins to sink in fear, but Hopeful holds up his head, calling, “I can feel the bottom, and it is solid!” Christian remembers God’s promise to be with him in the waters, they cross safely, and they are welcomed through the golden gate as every bell in the City rings for joy. The big idea: God is with us all the way, even to the very end, and the road of trusting him leads us home.

memory_verse.text: When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.

activity.title: Map of the Whole Journey
activity.materials: A long sheet of paper (or several sheets laid end to end) and crayons
steps: Lay the paper out on a table or the floor and draw a winding road from one end to the other.
At the start, draw the City of Destruction; at the far end, the river and the golden City.
Let each child choose a place from the twelve weeks — the swamp, the gate, the Cross, the lions, Doubting Castle — and draw it along the road.
Walk the map together from beginning to end, naming each place and what Christian learned there.
Finish by ringing pretend bells and cheering, “Christian is home!”
